analysis.one_liner: Bans pricing algorithms trained on competitors' secret data and requires companies to disclose when algorithms set prices or pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 9 Senate Democrats, has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal to use or sell a pricing algorithm that is trained on competitors' nonpublic data — the kind of shared data that lets software quietly nudge many companies toward the same higher prices. It creates a presumption of illegal price-fixing when one pricing tool is used by multiple competitors in the same market, with penalties that can reach thousands of dollars per day or the full price of everything sold with the algorithm. Companies with $5 million or more in revenue would have to tell customers, workers, and contractors when an algorithm sets their price or pay, including when that algorithm charges different people different prices. The FTC and Justice Department could demand audits of any pricing algorithm, and the FTC would publish a two-year study on how widely these tools are used.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers. When many competitors feed their private pricing data into the same software, prices across hotels, rentals, and other markets can climb together without any explicit agreement; banning that data-sharing targets the mechanism behind those price increases. Workers are covered too, because the bill defines 'price' to include pay for employees and contractors, so the same rules reach algorithmic wage-setting. Businesses competing on their own merits also benefit from a rule that stops rivals from coordinating through shared software.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to use or distribute any pricing algorithm that uses, incorporates, or was trained with nonpublic competitor data, with civil penalties of at least $10,000 per day (inflation-adjusted) or the full price of every product or service sold using the algorithm in violation. [S2]

Creates a presumption of an illegal agreement under the Sherman Act when a pricing algorithm is distributed to or used by two or more competitors in the same market, making it far easier to prove algorithmic price-fixing, with joint and several liability for distributors that knew the tool used competitor data. [S2]

Requires companies with $5 million or more in annual revenue to disclose to customers before purchase, and to employees and contractors, when an algorithm sets or recommends their price or pay — including when it charges different customers or pays different workers different amounts for the same thing. [S2]

Lets the Justice Department and FTC demand a certified report, under penalty of perjury by senior officers, explaining how any pricing algorithm works, what data trains it, and whether it discriminates among customers or workers. [S2]

Requires the FTC to study and publish findings within two years on how prevalent pricing algorithms are, how often they produce price or wage discrimination, and what sectors may need more oversight. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sell pricing software and large businesses that rely on it — hotels, landlords, airlines, e-commerce sellers, and platforms that use algorithmic pricing or pay-setting — would bear compliance costs, disclosure obligations, and new legal exposure. Some efficiency gains from algorithmic pricing (faster matching of supply and demand) could be lost when tools rely on pooled competitor data.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pricing software vendors and big algorithmic-price users

drawbacks.text: The ban is broad: it prohibits any algorithm trained with nonpublic competitor data, and the bill's own FTC study is tasked with weighing 'potential benefits or efficiencies of pricing algorithms,' an acknowledgment that these tools can also lower prices or improve matching; a sweeping ban could sacrifice some of those gains. [S2]

The definitions reach far beyond classic price-fixing — 'price' includes employee and contractor pay, and 'nonpublic data' includes anonymized data — so ordinary business tools that learn from aggregated market information could face penalties of $10,000 or more per day, a compliance burden that falls hardest on mid-sized firms near the $5 million disclosure threshold. [S2]

The presumption of an agreement and joint-and-several liability could expose software distributors and their customers to Sherman Act damages even without proof of intent to fix prices, raising the risk of costly litigation over legitimate pricing tools. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core target is real: software that pools competitors' private data can push many supposedly independent companies toward the same higher prices or lower pay, which current antitrust law struggles to reach because there is no paper agreement. The bill attacks that gap directly and adds transparency for consumers and workers. The trade-off is overbreadth — the definitions could sweep in legitimate tools that use aggregated or anonymized market data, and the penalty structure is aggressive. A carefully drafted version could capture the harm while sparing efficient uses; as written, some legitimate pricing software would likely be caught.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, joined by eight other Senate Democrats as cosponsors. [S2]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day. [S4]
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral. [S4]
All nine sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republican has signed on. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that sell and rely on algorithmic pricing tools, and any businesses that benefit from competitors' data flowing into shared pricing software, are better off so far, since the restrictions never advanced. Consumers and workers continue to pay prices and accept pay rates set by tools the bill would have restricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Algorithmic pricing vendors and their business customers

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; the bill sits in a committee controlled by the Republican majority. [S3] [S4]

industries.note: These firms sell or license the pricing algorithms the bill would regulate; distributing a tool trained on competitors' nonpublic data could trigger penalties and joint liability for Sherman Act violations. Their business depends on the data-pooling the bill bans. [S2]

industries.industry: Hotels, airlines, and short-term rental operators
industries.note: Heavy users of algorithmic revenue-management pricing; they would face disclosure duties to customers, audit demands, and legal exposure if their tools rely on pooled competitor data. The bill targets pricing practices in exactly these markets. [S2]

Rent-setting software has drawn scrutiny for coordinating rents across competing properties; the bill would make using tools trained on other landlords' nonpublic data unlawful and require disclosure that an algorithm set the rent. [S2]

industries.industry: Gig platforms and large employers using pay algorithms
industries.note: Because the bill defines 'price' to include employee and contractor pay, algorithmic wage-setting tools would be covered, with disclosure duties to workers and penalties for tools trained on competitors' data. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action in roughly a year, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee this Congress. Most single-party antitrust bills introduced in the Senate die in committee without a vote, and this one shows every sign of following that path unless it picks up bipartisan support.
